Jim stood in the center of the advanced yoga studio, his face a mask of determination and impending doom. The instructor, a serene woman named Serenity, glided into a complex inversion. "Now," she whispered, "find your center."

Jim tried to find his center, but his center was currently located somewhere near his left knee, which was screaming in protest. He attempted to mimic the pose, a twisted variation of the Eagle Pose, but ended up looking less like a yogi and more like a confused giraffe trying to untangle its own legs.

The room was silent, save for the soft breathing of twelve advanced practitioners. Then, Jim shifted his weight. A sound erupted from his posterior—a long, resonant *toot* that echoed off the mirrored walls like a foghorn in a library.

Serenity froze. Her eye twitched.

Jim, oblivious, grunted as he tried to correct his balance. Another sound followed, this one higher-pitched and squeaky, like a rubber duck being stepped on by an elephant.

The class struggled. One man in the back bit his lip so hard he drew blood. A woman in the front row closed her eyes tightly, tears of suppressed laughter streaming down her cheeks. They were trying to maintain their zen, but the air was thick with the scent of embarrassment and the auditory chaos of Jim’s digestive distress.

Jim, sensing the tension, thought he was doing well. "I feel... aligned," he wheezed, attempting a final twist.

As he twisted, he accidentally bumped into the person next to him, who happened to be holding a large, inflated yoga ball. The ball rolled away, hitting a stack of mats, which toppled over, landing on a water cooler. Water sprayed everywhere.

In the chaos, Jim slipped. As he fell, he let out a final, triumphant grunt that sounded suspiciously like a trumpet blast.

The class erupted. Not in anger, but in uncontrollable, hysterical laughter. Serenity, the picture of zen, finally cracked, laughing so hard she fell out of her pose and landed in a heap of mats.

Jim lay on the floor, covered in water, surrounded by laughing yogis. He looked up at the ceiling, defeated but oddly proud. "Well," he muttered, "at least I found my center. It was just in the wrong place."
